questions.stem: Which of the following best defines inflation?

options.option_text: A one-time increase in the price of a single commodity
A sustained rise in the general price level of goods and services in an economy
A decrease in the production of goods
An increase in the nominal value of currency

questions.explanation: Inflation is a SUSTAINED rise in the GENERAL price level — not a one-off change or a sectoral change. It erodes the purchasing power of money: the same rupee buys fewer goods over time. Measured via indices like CPI and WPI. A single commodity's price rise (e.g., tomatoes in monsoon) is NOT inflation if average prices are stable. An increase in nominal currency value is the opposite (deflation/currency strengthening).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: In India, which of the following is the primary inflation index used by the RBI for its monetary policy decisions?

options.option_text: WPI (Wholesale Price Index)
CPI-Combined (Consumer Price Index)
CPI-IW (Industrial Workers)
IIP (Index of Industrial Production)

questions.explanation: Since 2014 (Urjit Patel Committee + 2016 Monetary Policy Framework Agreement), the RBI targets HEADLINE CPI-Combined (released by NSO/MoSPI) with a central target of 4% ± 2%. WPI (Office of Economic Adviser, DPIIT) is used for deflating GDP at constant prices and tracking producer prices, but NOT as the RBI's policy target. CPI-IW (Labour Bureau) is used for DA calculations for govt employees, not RBI targeting.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of 'cost-push' inflation?

options.option_text: A boom in consumer demand during a festival
A sharp increase in crude oil prices raising transport and production costs
Government printing excess money
A stock market rally

questions.explanation: COST-PUSH inflation arises when input costs (raw materials, wages, fuel) rise and producers pass this on to consumers. Classic example: oil shocks (1973 OPEC crisis, 2008 oil spike). DEMAND-PULL inflation arises when aggregate demand exceeds supply (option A — festival demand surge). Excess money printing is typically classified as demand-pull/monetary inflation (option C). A stock rally is asset-price inflation, not general inflation.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: What is the current inflation target band set for the RBI under the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement?

options.option_text: 6% (hard ceiling)

questions.explanation: The RBI's flexible inflation targeting framework sets a MEDIUM-TERM target of 4% CPI-Combined, with a tolerance band of ±2 percentage points (lower bound 2%, upper bound 6%). This was first set in 2016 (initial 5-year review) and was retained at the March 2021 review for another 5 years (2021-26). If inflation breaches the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government explaining reasons and remedial actions.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Galloping inflation refers to inflation of:

options.option_text: 0 to 3% annually
3 to 10% annually
10 to 1000% annually
Below 0% (deflation)

questions.explanation: Inflation categories: (1) Creeping/Mild — <3%; (2) Walking/Trotting — 3-10%; (3) GALLOPING/Running — 10-1000%; (4) Hyperinflation — >1000% per year (e.g., Weimar Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008, Venezuela 2018). Galloping inflation disrupts business planning and wage contracts. Deflation is NEGATIVE inflation (falling prices) and is generally considered a warning sign of slump.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a MONETARY POLICY tool that the RBI uses to control inflation?

options.option_text: Raising or lowering Income Tax rates
Changing the Repo Rate
Issuing Union Government bonds
Adjusting MSP for agricultural commodities

questions.explanation: MONETARY policy tools are used by the CENTRAL BANK (RBI). Key tools: Repo Rate, Reverse Repo Rate, MSF, Bank Rate, CRR, SLR, OMO (Open Market Operations). Changing Repo Rate (lending rate for banks to RBI) influences bank interest rates → consumer borrowing/saving → aggregate demand → inflation. Income Tax is a FISCAL POLICY tool (Finance Ministry). Government bonds are fiscal. MSP is set by Cabinet on CACP recommendation — neither monetary nor a direct fiscal tool.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: High growth with rising prices
Low/stagnant growth accompanied by high inflation and unemployment
Declining prices with rising output
Stable prices combined with zero unemployment

questions.explanation: STAGFLATION = STAGnation + inFLATION. It is the coexistence of (1) slow/zero economic growth, (2) high inflation, and (3) elevated unemployment. It challenges the classical Phillips-curve view that inflation and unemployment trade off. Famous example: US in 1970s during oil shocks. Policymakers face a dilemma: tightening money controls inflation but worsens unemployment; loosening controls does the opposite.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The business cycle typically consists of four phases. Which phase is characterized by declining output, rising unemployment, and falling prices?

options.option_text: Expansion
Peak
Contraction/Recession
Trough

questions.explanation: Business cycle phases: (1) EXPANSION — GDP rising, employment up, prices rising modestly; (2) PEAK — growth at maximum, economy overheated; (3) CONTRACTION/RECESSION — GDP falling, unemployment rising, prices falling or rising slowly; (4) TROUGH — economy at its bottom before recovery. A recession is technically defined as TWO consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth (NBER uses broader criteria). Great Depression (1929-33) was a severe contraction.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes 'core inflation'?

options.option_text: Inflation in all goods and services
Inflation excluding food and fuel
Inflation only in essential commodities
Inflation faced by rural consumers only

questions.explanation: CORE INFLATION strips out volatile items (food and fuel) from headline CPI to reveal underlying inflation trends driven by broader demand-supply conditions. Food/fuel are excluded because they swing due to monsoons, crude shocks, etc. — noise that obscures the inflation signal. Central banks watch core inflation closely since it responds more predictably to monetary policy. In India, core is often quoted alongside headline in RBI bi-monthly reviews. i.e., non-volatile components.

questions.stem: Who chairs the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), which decides the repo rate?

options.option_text: The Prime Minister
The Finance Minister
The Governor of the RBI
The Chief Economic Advisor

questions.explanation: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has 6 members: 3 from RBI (Governor, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one officer nominated by RBI Central Board) + 3 external members (nominated by the Government of India for 4-year terms). The RBI Governor CHAIRS the MPC and has a CASTING VOTE in case of a tie. The MPC meets at least 4 times a year (usually 6) and decisions are made by majority vote. The PM and FM have no direct vote.

questions.stem: The term 'disinflation' is correctly used to describe which of the following economic situations?

options.option_text: Prices fall sharply and persistently over several quarters
The rate of inflation slows down while prices still continue to rise
The economy records exactly zero percent inflation for a full year
Negative price growth contracts economic output across all sectors

questions.explanation: Disinflation means the rate of inflation is falling — prices are still rising, just more slowly. For example, inflation dropping from 8% to 4% is disinflation. Option A describes deflation (absolute price fall), not disinflation. Option C (zero inflation) is price stability, not disinflation. Confusing disinflation with deflation is a classic exam trap.

questions.stem: India revised the base year for computing the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) in 2017. What is the current base year in use?

options.option_text: 2004-05, the series preceding the 2017 DPIIT revision
2011-12, adopted by the Office of the Economic Adviser
2017-18, aligned with the revised National Accounts Series
2001-02, used under the earlier CSO computation framework

questions.explanation: India's WPI base year was revised from 2004-05 to 2011-12 effective April 2017, carried out by the Office of the Economic Adviser (OEA) under the Ministry of Commerce & Industry. Option A (2004-05) is the old base year candidates commonly confuse with the current one. 2017-18 and 2001-02 have never been official WPI base years.

questions.stem: The original Phillips Curve, proposed by A.W. Phillips in 1958, established an empirical inverse relationship between which two macroeconomic variables?

options.option_text: Nominal interest rates and broad money supply growth rate
Unemployment rate and the rate of nominal wage inflation
Real GDP growth rate and the aggregate consumer price level
Real interest rates and gross fixed capital formation trends

questions.explanation: Phillips (1958) studied UK data 1861–1957 and found that low unemployment correlated with high wage inflation, and vice versa — a trade-off. The curve was later adapted to show unemployment vs price inflation broadly. Options A and D describe liquidity preference and investment theories respectively, while Option C conflates the Phillips curve with the aggregate demand-supply framework.

questions.stem: In India's Consumer Price Index (CPI Combined) basket, which major expenditure group carries the single highest weight, making it the dominant driver of headline inflation?

options.option_text: Housing, including rent and maintenance charges (10.07%)
Food and beverages, covering cereals, pulses and proteins (45.86%)
Clothing, footwear and allied textile products (6.53%)
Fuel and light, including firewood, chips and dung cake (6.84%)

questions.explanation: Food and beverages has a weight of ~45.86% in India's CPI Combined basket (base year 2012), which is why vegetable price spikes — onion, tomato — cause sharp headline CPI movements even when other components are stable. Housing (10.07%) is the next largest single sub-group. Candidates frequently over-estimate fuel's weight since it politically dominates headlines.

questions.stem: When an economy's aggregate demand consistently exceeds its full-employment output level, Keynesian theory describes this excess as producing which specific condition?

options.option_text: Deflationary gap, caused by excess household saving over investment
Recessionary gap, driven by collapse in consumer confidence nationally
Inflationary gap, where demand-pull pressure bids up the price level
Structural gap, arising from supply-side bottlenecks in key industries

questions.explanation: An inflationary gap exists when actual aggregate demand exceeds the potential (full-employment) output — producers cannot expand real output fast enough, so prices rise instead. A deflationary/recessionary gap is the opposite: actual output falls short of potential. Option A incorrectly calls it a 'deflationary gap'; Options B and D describe entirely different phenomena (demand collapse and structural constraints).

questions.stem: The Fisher Effect in monetary economics predicts that, holding the real interest rate constant at 4%, a sustained rise in expected inflation from 2% to 6% will cause the nominal interest rate to move approximately to:

options.option_text: 4%, since the real rate is immune to changes in inflation expectations
10%, the sum of the 4% real rate and the new 6% expected inflation
6%, where the inflation premium replaces rather than adds to real rate
8%, reflecting compounding between the real rate and the inflation gap

questions.explanation: Fisher Equation: Nominal rate ≈ Real rate + Expected inflation. With real rate = 4% and expected inflation = 6%, nominal rate ≈ 10%. The key insight is that lenders demand compensation for expected purchasing-power loss ON TOP OF the real return — not instead of it (ruling out Option C). Option D (8%) arises from incorrectly using only the 4-percentage-point rise in inflation rather than the full new expected inflation level.

questions.stem: Selective Credit Controls (SCCs) imposed by the RBI — such as minimum margins for lending against specific commodities like pulses or oilseeds — are classified under which category of monetary instruments?

options.option_text: Quantitative instruments, as they cap the overall volume of bank credit
Qualitative instruments, targeting the direction and purpose of credit
Automatic stabilisers that activate without any RBI discretionary action
Open market operations involving RBI's secondary-market bond purchases

questions.explanation: Qualitative (selective) credit controls regulate WHERE and FOR WHAT credit flows — not how much total credit exists. SCCs like higher margins, interest rate ceilings on sensitive commodities, and directives under Section 21/35-A of the Banking Regulation Act are classic qualitative tools aimed at preventing hoarding-driven commodity inflation. Option A describes quantitative tools like CRR/SLR/Repo which affect total credit quantity. Automatic stabilisers (Option C) are fiscal concepts — taxes, unemployment benefits — not RBI interventions.
